opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the decision didn't come from one moment. It built up over several years of research.

During my PhD at Stanford, I worked mostly on 3D vision: understanding objects, their poses, their parts, how they can be articulated. At some point I started asking myself what all this perception is ultimately for. Recognizing a mug or estimating a drawer's pose is interesting, but its real value shows up when an agent can act on that understanding: open the drawer, pick up the mug, put it somewhere useful. So my interest naturally moved from seeing the world to interacting with it, which is embodied intelligence.

When I came back to China and started my own lab, I had to think about the long-term question: if I'm going to spend ten or twenty years on something, what's the scenario that's both scientifically deepest and most meaningful to society? Factories are important, but they're relatively structured, and traditional automation already handles a lot there. The home is the opposite. It's open-ended, unstructured, full of long-tail objects and tasks, and every home is different. If you can make a robot work reliably in a home, you've basically solved generalization, which is the core problem of embodied AI. So scientifically, it's the hardest and most honest test.

Then there's the societal side. China, like many countries, faces an aging population. There will be a huge need for help with elderly care, housework, and daily assistance, and not enough people to provide it. A general-purpose home robot isn't just a cool demo. It could change how millions of families live. That gave me a strong sense of mission.

I also felt the timing was right. A few things were converging: large models giving robots much better semantic understanding and reasoning, progress in simulation and synthetic data so we no longer depend only on expensive real-world data collection, and China's hardware supply chain making capable robot bodies much cheaper than before. Ten years ago, home robotics would have felt like a dream. Now I think it's a hard but realistic engineering and scientific path.

Of course, I'm very clear that it's a long road. Home robots won't arrive overnight. We'll probably go step by step, first proving generalizable manipulation in commercial settings like retail or pharmacies, then gradually moving toward the home. But I wanted the north star to be the home, because that's where the hardest problems and the biggest impact both are.

r001.rationale: The response cites converging technology and the right timing, but does not identify pursuing the next technological wave as He Wang’s motivation.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss funding or starting a company, so it does not state that funding alone was insufficient motivation.

fable-5.1.text:
When I came back and had to decide what to commit myself to for the next ten or twenty years, I didn't start from "what paper can I publish next." I started from a much more naive question: if embodied intelligence actually works, where does it change ordinary people's lives the most?

A lot of my background was in 3D vision and manipulation, and the natural path would have been to go into factories or logistics, where the environment is structured and you can get something working fairly quickly. But I kept coming back to the home. The home is the hardest environment there is. Nothing is standardized. Every kitchen is different, every cup is placed differently, there are children and pets and clutter, and the robot has to deal with objects it has never seen before. If you can make a robot that is genuinely useful in a home, you have essentially solved generalization, and that is the core scientific problem I care about. So the home was not a compromise. It was the place where the research question and the real need overlap most completely.

The second consideration was timing. When I was abroad, I watched the shift happen in language and vision, where scale and data suddenly made things possible that looked decades away. I was fairly convinced the same transition would come to robotics, and that the bottleneck would be data and generalizable representations rather than better controllers. If that is true, the home is also the place with the largest long-term data flywheel, because that is where robots would eventually be living with people around the clock.

And the third factor was honestly about China. Our aging population is arriving quickly. The number of people who will need help with daily living, with elderly care, is enormous, and there will not be enough human caregivers. That makes home robotics not just an interesting research topic but something with real urgency here. Returning meant I could do work that is both scientifically foundational and tied to a problem my own society is going to face. That combination is what made the decision feel stable to me, even knowing it would take a long time and that many of the early years would look like slow progress from the outside.

r001.rationale: He Wang says he expected the shift driven by scale and data to reach robotics and chose home robotics with that transition in mind.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention funding or starting a company, so it does not state that funding alone was insufficient motivation.

astra-6.text:
For me, the appeal of home robotics was that it connected a long-term research challenge with something people could use in everyday life. If we want robots to be useful in homes, they have to deal with a world that hasn’t been carefully arranged for them. Objects move, rooms are different, and even a simple request can involve a lot of uncertainty.

That makes it a difficult research direction, but also a compelling one. It brings perception, learning, and physical interaction together: a robot has to understand enough about its surroundings to actually do something useful.

So I thought about it less as choosing one particular product and more as choosing a problem that could guide years of work. The long-term ambition is broad, but you can make progress through concrete tasks and ask, at each step, whether the robot is becoming more capable and reliable in everyday environments.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes everyday usefulness and the research challenge of home robotics, but does not say He Wang chose it to pursue the next technological wave.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention funding, starting a company, or whether funding alone would motivate him.

sol-6.1.text:
When I returned to China, I asked myself what kind of problem I would be willing to work on for the next ten or twenty years. Home robotics appealed to me because it brings together a lot of fundamental challenges: perception, learning, manipulation, and making decisions in an environment that keeps changing.

A home is much less structured than a factory. Objects are in different places, every household is different, and people don’t always give precise instructions. Getting a robot to be useful in that setting requires more than making one demonstration work. It has to adapt.

That combination attracted me: there are deep research questions, but also a very concrete purpose—helping people with everyday tasks. I saw it as a direction where the scientific work and the practical goal could support each other over the long term.

r001.rationale: The response says home robotics appealed because of its research challenges and practical purpose, but does not identify pursuing the next technological wave as He Wang’s motivation.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention funding or starting a company, so it does not state that funding alone was insufficient motivation.
